"'''Believe'''" is a song by the American singer [[Cher]] from her 22nd studio album, ''[[Believe (Cher album)|Believe]]'' (1998). It was released as the [[lead single]] on October 19, 1998, by [[Warner Bros. Records]]. After circulating for months, a [[demo (music)|demo]] written by [[Brian Higgins (producer)|Brian Higgins]], Matthew Gray, Stuart McLennen and [[Tim Powell (producer)|Timothy Powell]] was submitted to Warner's chairman, [[Rob Dickins]], while he was scouting for songs to include on Cher's new album. Aside from the chorus, Dickins was not impressed by the track so he enlisted two more writers, Steve Torch and [[Paul Barry (songwriter)|Paul Barry]], to complete it. Cher contributed some lyrics but did not receive any songwriting credit. Recording took place at Dreamhouse Studio in [[West London]], while production was handled by [[Mark Taylor (music producer)|Mark Taylor]] and [[Brian Rawling]].

"Believe" is an upbeat [[dance-pop]] and [[electropop]] song and departed from Cher's previous music. It featured a pioneering use of the audio processing software [[Auto-Tune]] to distort her vocals, which was widely imitated and became known as the "Cher effect". The lyrics describe empowerment and self-sufficiency after a painful breakup. "Believe" received positive reviews; critics praised its production and catchiness, with some deeming it a highlight from the album. The song has been listed as one of Cher's most important releases. At the [[42nd Annual Grammy Awards]], it was nominated for [[Grammy Award for Record of the Year|Record of the Year]] and won [[Grammy Award for Best Dance Recording|Best Dance Recording]], the first and only Grammy Award that Cher has won.

"Believe" topped the [[record chart]]s in over 23 countries and has sold more than 11 million copies worldwide. It is Cher's most successful single, and one of the [[List of best-selling singles|best-selling singles in music history]]. "Believe" was the biggest-selling song of 1998 in the United Kingdom, and remains the [[List of best-selling singles in the United Kingdom|highest-selling single by a solo female artist]] there. In the United States, it was Cher's fifth number-one single on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] chart, and it topped the [[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1999|Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1999]]. The accompanying music video (directed by [[Nigel Dick]]) was nominated for [[MTV Video Music Award for Best Dance Video|Best Dance Video]] at the [[1999 MTV Video Music Awards]].

Cher has performed the song on many occasions, including the [[1999 Brit Awards]], the [[Sanremo Music Festival]], as well as on several talk shows and variety programs (in America and abroad). It has since become a fan favorite, and a staple in the setlist of her [[List of Cher concert tours|concert tours]]. "Believe" has been [[Cover version|covered]] by numerous artists, and it's also been sung or referenced in several feature films and scripted TV shows. Scholars and academics noted the way in which Cher was able to re-invent herself, and yet stay true to her image, while still being able to release music that was fresh and contemporary amidst the more "[[teen pop]]"-based music of the period.{{Citation needed|date=July 2026|reason=Which scholars and academics?}} They also credited the song for restoring Cher's social popularity and further cementing her position as a [[pop icon]]. "Believe" earned Cher a place in the ''[[Guinness World Records|Guinness Book of World Records]]'', and ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' listed it among the "[[Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs of All Time|500 Greatest Songs of All Time]]".

sections.wikitext:
The origins of the song go back to as early as 1991, when the original demo of "Believe", written by singer Mark Scott and songwriter [[Brian Higgins (producer)|Brian Higgins]] and co-produced by [[Nick Van Eede]] and [[Kevin MacMichael]] (both of the band [[Cutting Crew]]) was created for [[Warner Records]], to which Van Eede and MacMichael received modest compensation—reportedly just a bottle of whisky—for their contributions. The demo was passed on to several major artists through Higgins and eventually landed with Cher in 1997 which was rearranged with altered lyrics.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.smoothradio.com/features/the-story-of/cher-believe-lyrics-meaning-video-facts/|title=The Story Of… 'Believe' by Cher|website=[[Smooth Radio (2014)|Smooth]]}}</ref> This rearranged demo of "Believe", now written by Higgins, Matthew Gray, Stuart McLennen and [[Tim Powell (producer)|Timothy Powell]], circulated at Warner Records for months. Higgins offered the demo to the English [[indie dance]] band [[Saint Etienne (band)|Saint Etienne]], who turned it down.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2025/may/30/saint-etienne-interview-final-album-international|work=[[The Guardian]]|title='We want to stop in our prime': Saint Etienne on their final album, turning down Cher's Believe, and why pop is a dying art|first=Fergal|last=Kinney|date=May 30, 2025|access-date=May 30, 2025}}</ref> According to the producer [[Mark Taylor (music producer)|Mark Taylor]], "everyone loved the chorus" but not the rest.<ref name="SOS" /> The Warner chairman, [[Rob Dickins]], asked the production house Dreamhouse to work on it; their goal was to make a [[Dance music|dance]] record that would not alienate Cher fans.<ref name="SOS">{{cite web|url=https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/recording-cher-believe|title=Recording Cher's 'Believe'|first=Sue|last=Sillitoe|date=February 1999|work=[[Sound on Sound]]|access-date=December 27, 2018}} (updated with Historical Footnote)</ref> Two more writers, Steve Torch and [[Paul Barry (songwriter)|Paul Barry]], completed a version that Dickins and Cher were happy with.<ref name="SOS" />

Cher felt the song was "too whiny" and wanted to "toughen it up a bit".<ref name="Bego20042">{{cite book|first=Mark|last=Bego|title=Cher: If You Believe|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XIQcOufdLVUC&pg=PA283|date=July 15, 2004|publisher=Taylor Trade Publishing|isbn=978-1-4616-2592-6|pages=283–}}</ref> Feeling that "a girl can be sad in one verse, but she can't be sad in two verses",<ref name="Farber-20232">{{cite web |last=Farber|first=Jim|date=October 18, 2023|title=Cher: 'My life seems to be longer than any other human being ever'|url=https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2023/oct/18/cher-interview-christmas-album|access-date=December 1, 2023|work=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> she rewrote the lyrics in the second verse to make the character more assertive: 'I need time to move on, I need love to feel strong / 'Cause I've had time to think it through and maybe I'm too good for you".<ref name="Farber-20232" /><ref name=":0">{{cite news |last=Strauss|first=Neil|date=March 11, 1999|title=Cher resurrected, again, by a hit; the long, hard but serendipitous road to 'Believe'|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/03/11/arts/cher-resurrected-again-by-a-hit-the-long-hard-but-serendipitous-road-to-believe.html?pagewanted=all|access-date=January 15, 2018|work=[[The New York Times]]|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name="The 500 Greatest Songs of All Time2">{{Cite magazine |date=September 15, 2021|title=The 500 Greatest Songs of All Time|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/best-songs-of-all-time-1224767/cher-believe-2-1225001/|magazine=[[Rolling Stone]]|access-date=May 30, 2025}}</ref> In 2023, Cher said she regretted not asking for a songwriting credit.<ref name="Farber-20232" />

The origins of the song go back to as early as 1991, when the original demo of "Believe", written by singer Mark Scott and songwriter Brian Higgins and co-produced by Nick Van Eede and Kevin MacMichael (both of the band Cutting Crew) was created for Warner Records, to which Van Eede and MacMichael received modest compensation—reportedly just a bottle of whisky—for their contributions. The demo was passed on to several major artists through Higgins and eventually landed with Cher in 1997 which was rearranged with altered lyrics. This rearranged demo of "Believe", now written by Higgins, Matthew Gray, Stuart McLennen and Timothy Powell, circulated at Warner Records for months. Higgins offered the demo to the English indie dance band Saint Etienne, who turned it down. According to the producer Mark Taylor, "everyone loved the chorus" but not the rest. The Warner chairman, Rob Dickins, asked the production house Dreamhouse to work on it; their goal was to make a dance record that would not alienate Cher fans. Two more writers, Steve Torch and Paul Barry, completed a version that Dickins and Cher were happy with.

Cher felt the song was "too whiny" and wanted to "toughen it up a bit". Feeling that "a girl can be sad in one verse, but she can't be sad in two verses", she rewrote the lyrics in the second verse to make the character more assertive: 'I need time to move on, I need love to feel strong / 'Cause I've had time to think it through and maybe I'm too good for you". In 2023, Cher said she regretted not asking for a songwriting credit.

sections.heading: Recording
sections.wikitext:
"Believe" was recorded in mid-1998 at the Dreamhouse studio operated by Metro Productions in [[Kingston upon Thames]], London. It was assembled with [[Cubase]] on an early [[Power Macintosh G3]], with synthesizers including a [[Clavia|Clavia Nord Rack]] and an [[Oberheim Matrix synthesizers|Oberheim Matrix 1000]]. Cher's vocals were recorded on three [[DA-88|TASCAM DA-88]] digital audio recorders with a [[Georg Neumann|Neumann U67]] microphone.<ref name="SOS" /><ref name=":0" />

Cher's vocals were processed using the [[pitch correction]] software [[Auto-Tune]]. Auto-Tune was designed to be used subtly to correct sharp or flat notes in vocal performances; however, Taylor used extreme settings to create unnaturally rapid corrections, thereby removing [[portamento]], the natural slide between pitches in singing.<ref name="Frere-Jones-20082">{{cite magazine |last=Frere-Jones|first=Sasha|author1-link=Sasha Frere-Jones|date=June 9, 2008|title=The Gerbil's Revenge|url=http://www.newyorker.com/arts/critics/musical/2008/06/09/080609crmu_music_frerejones?currentPage=1|access-date=May 30, 2012|magazine=[[The New Yorker]]|publisher=[[Condé Nast]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080609085147/http://www.newyorker.com/arts/critics/musical/2008/06/09/080609crmu_music_frerejones?currentPage=all<!-- https://archive.today/20241227164744/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2008/06/09/the-gerbils-revenge -->|archive-date=2008-06-09<!-- 27 December 2024 -->}}</ref> Taylor said it was "the most nerve-wracking part of the project", as he was not sure how Cher would react.<ref name="SOS" /> She insisted the effect remain when Warner wanted it removed.<ref name=":0" /> In an attempt to protect their method, the producers initially claimed it was achieved using a [[vocoder]].<ref name="SOS" /> The manual for Auto-Tune's fifth version describes the zero-speed setting as the "Cher effect".<ref name="Frere-Jones-20082" />

"Believe" was recorded in mid-1998 at the Dreamhouse studio operated by Metro Productions in Kingston upon Thames, London. It was assembled with Cubase on an early Power Macintosh G3, with synthesizers including a Clavia Nord Rack and an Oberheim Matrix 1000. Cher's vocals were recorded on three TASCAM DA-88 digital audio recorders with a Neumann U67 microphone.

Cher's vocals were processed using the pitch correction software Auto-Tune. Auto-Tune was designed to be used subtly to correct sharp or flat notes in vocal performances; however, Taylor used extreme settings to create unnaturally rapid corrections, thereby removing portamento, the natural slide between pitches in singing. Taylor said it was "the most nerve-wracking part of the project", as he was not sure how Cher would react. She insisted the effect remain when Warner wanted it removed. In an attempt to protect their method, the producers initially claimed it was achieved using a vocoder. The manual for Auto-Tune's fifth version describes the zero-speed setting as the "Cher effect".

sections.heading: Composition
sections.wikitext:
Critics described "Believe" as [[Eurodance]],<ref name="stereogum2">{{cite web |title=The Number Ones: Cher's "Believe"|url=https://www.stereogum.com/2191750/the-number-ones-chers-believe/columns/the-number-ones/|author=Tom Breihan|date=July 4, 2022|publisher=Stereogum}}</ref> [[Europop]],<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/2024/apr/22/cher-ozzy-osbourne-tribe-called-quest-2024-rock-and-roll-hall-of-fame-inductees|title=Cher, Ozzy Osbourne and A Tribe Called Quest among 2024 Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductees|work=The Guardian|date=December 26, 2024|last1=Beaumont-Thomas|first1=Ben}}</ref> [[Dance music|dance]],<ref name="stereogum2" /> [[dance-pop]] and [[electropop]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.musictimes.com/articles/4761/20140313/throwback-thursday-believe-cher-song-brought-auto-tune-listen.htm|title=Throwback Thursday: 'Believe' by Cher, the song that brought you Auto-Tune [LISTEN]|work=Music Times|date=March 13, 2014|access-date=October 14, 2015}}</ref><ref name="about" /><ref name="RSguide2">{{cite book|last=Hunter|first=James|chapter=Cher|editor1-last=Brackett|editor1-first=Nathan|editor2-last=Hoard|editor2-first=Christian|date=November 2, 2004|title=The New Rolling Stone Album Guide|publisher=Simon & Schuster|location=New York|pages=159}}</ref> It was recorded in the [[Key (music)|key]] of [[F-sharp major|F{{sharp}} major]] with a [[tempo]] of 133 beats per minute. It follows a [[chord progression]] of F{{sharp}}–C{{sharp}}–G{{sharp}}m–B–F{{sharp}}–A{{sharp}}m<small>7</small>–G{{sharp}}m–D{{sharp}}m, and Cher's vocals span from F{{sharp}}<sub>3</sub> to C{{sharp}}<sub>5</sub>.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Believe|url=http://www.musicnotes.com/sheetmusic/mtd.asp?ppn=MN0048844_U1|website=www.musicnotes.com|date=February 14, 2005|access-date=January 2, 2016}}</ref>

In the verses, Cher's vocals are manipulated heavily with Auto-Tune. The ''New Yorker'' said this produced "a controlled version of losing control, hinting at various histrionic stations of the human voice". It was used more sparingly for the chorus, "Do you believe in life after love?", which is performed in a "a full, human-sounding voice".<ref name="Frere-Jones-20082" />

Bob Waliszewski of Plugged In said that Cher "musters self-confidence to deal with a failed romance". In 2018, Dave Fawbert from ShortList described "Believe" as a "really great pop song with, as ever, an absolute powerhouse vocal performance from Cher".

The music video for "Believe" was directed by [[Nigel Dick]]. It features Cher in a nightclub in a double role as both a singer on stage wearing a glowing headdress and a supernatural being in a cage surrounded by many people to whom she is giving advice. The video follows a woman (played by Katrine De Candole)<ref>Cher: Believe. IMDb. https://www.imdb.com/title/tt6725512/</ref> who is in the club with her friends and sees her ex-boyfriend. Scenes are shown of her clearly disappointed when he walks away from her and then proceeds to dance and make out with another woman in her presence.{{Citation needed|date=September 2025}} The version on ''[[The Very Best of Cher: The Video Hits Collection]]'' is slightly different from the previous version (which is also included on the Mallay Believe Bonus VCD) with additional scenes towards the end that were not in the original video. There are also two "rough" versions of the video as the song was released in Europe before a video was completed.{{Citation needed|date=September 2025}} The first is a compilation of scenes from the videos of Cher's previous singles "One by One" and "Walking in Memphis" and the second includes a brief scene of the "Believe" video where Cher sings the chorus while the rest of the video is composed of scenes from "One by One".{{Citation needed|date=September 2025}}

The ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' music critic [[Chuck Taylor (music journalist)|Chuck Taylor]] in March 1999 graded the video a "C", praising Cher's appearance but criticizing "an unnecessary subplot about a few kids stalking each other."<ref>{{Cite magazine |title=When Sound and Vision Collide: We Rate the Videos Behind Radio's Current Hits |date=March 6, 1999 |magazine=Billboard |last=Taylor |first=Chuck |page=94 |issue=10 |volume=111 |issn=0006-2510 }} ProQuest document no. 1008145.</ref> In ''Pitchfork'', [[Simon Reynolds]] wrote that through the combination of cosmetic surgery, makeup and bright lights, "Cher actually ''looks'' how Auto-Tune sounds ... Her face and her voice seem to be made out of the same immaterial substance."<ref name="Pitchfork">{{cite web |author=Reynolds |first=Simon |author-link=Simon Reynolds |date=September 17, 2018 |title=How Auto-Tune revolutionized the sound of popular music |url=https://pitchfork.com/features/article/how-auto-tune-revolutionized-the-sound-of-popular-music/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190726001852/https://pitchfork.com/features/article/how-auto-tune-revolutionized-the-sound-of-popular-music/ |archive-date=July 26, 2019 |access-date=September 28, 2018 |work=[[Pitchfork (website)|Pitchfork]]}}</ref>
